chunks: Your approach to debug, test, validate. The question: What is your approach to debug/test/validate something?
The interviewer is not asking for a clever trick.

They want to hear a repeatable method: define what "working" means, reproduce the problem, gather evidence before changing anything, narrow it down, change one thing at a time, and confirm the real cause.
For validation, the method is the same but done in advance, against requirements.
A good answer sounds like a short story with a clear structure. A weak answer sounds like a list of random things you poked at.
The strong version says: here is what I expected, here is what I saw, here is how I cut the search in half each time, here is the cause I proved, and here is what I wrote down for the next person.
It should be about a real project of yours.
The debug loop. The back-arrow from "change one thing" to "hypothesize" is where most time is spent. The only exit is a fix you can switch on and off.
Root cause: the underlying reason for a failure, not just the visible symptom. Half-splitting: testing the middle of a chain so each test removes half the candidates.
Known-good unit: a working board to compare against. Regression test: a test run after a fix to check that nothing else broke.
Corner testing: testing at the extremes of voltage, temperature and load.
A skeleton answer. Replace the placeholders with your real experience. "On [project], [symptom] happened [how often]. I expected [spec or known-good behavior].
I reproduced it by [conditions]. I checked the cheap things first: [rails, clocks, reset].
To isolate it, I measured at the middle of the chain and found the problem was [upstream/downstream]. I changed one thing at a time.
When [change] fixed it, I removed it to confirm the failure returned. The root cause was [cause]. I documented it and added [test]."
Half-splitting is fast: a chain of 64 stages needs at most 6 tests, because 2 to the 6 equals 64 . That is the whole idea.
"My approach is a loop: define what correct looks like, reproduce the failure, gather evidence without changing things, then split the system in half to isolate it.
I rank hypotheses by likelihood and cost, test one variable at a time, and once something fixes it I verify I understand why and check for side effects. I document the root cause.
For validation I start from requirements, test corners and margin, automate it and look at the data distribution."
Quick check. You change a capacitor, update the firmware and re-seat a cable, and the fault disappears. What is the main problem with this approach?
